VIDEO.title: Is This the Parable That Got Jesus Killed?
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 21:23-46 · Episode 42 (#45 of 58 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 21:23-46. In the temple the chief priests and elders demand to know by what authority Jesus acts. He answers with a question about John's baptism, and when they refuse to answer, so does He. Then He tells two parables. In the first, a man's two sons are told to work in the vineyard: one says no but goes, the other says yes but does not. In the second, a landowner plants a vineyard, rents it to vine-growers, and sends slaves and finally his son, whom they kill. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, 'The stone which the builders rejected,' and says the kingdom of God will be taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruit. The leaders realize He is speaking about them.

The question about authority asks who gave Jesus the right to teach, the formal recognition of a rabbi. The crowds already saw that He taught as one having authority (7:28-29). Jesus points them to John, the prophet who baptized Him, and to the Father's voice from heaven.

'A man had two sons' was a known way to begin a story (Luke 15:11). The point: obedience, not words, is doing the will of the Father. Tax collectors and prostitutes, who said no and then repented, are entering the kingdom before the leaders.

The vineyard parable is built on Isaiah 5, where Israel is God's vineyard and God looks for justice and finds bloodshed. Here the problem is the vine-growers, the leaders. Psalm 118:22 turns the rejected son into the chief corner stone.

The lesson: to the one who knows God and obeys Him, Jesus Christ is the cornerstone of protection. To the one who refuses to know God and disobeys His will, Jesus Christ will be the source of punishment and destruction.
QUOTES: To the one who knows God and obeys him, Jesus Christ is the capstone or the cornerstone of protection.
Putting both parables together, the message becomes clear. It's doing the will of God.
Jesus indicts the ones who were supposed to care for this vineyard.
It reveals the dividing line between those who truly know God and those who only know religion.

method.h: Find the Old Testament story under the parable
method.p: Jesus' vineyard parable retells Isaiah 5:1-7 and ends with Psalm 118:22. Reading those first shows who the vineyard, the owner, the tenants and the son are.

LSB_QUOTES.text: By what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?
The stone which the builders rejected / Has become the chief corner stone.
Therefore as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him,

left.text: And when He entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to Him while He was teaching, and said, “By what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?”

right.text: for He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes.

lines.text: The day after He overturned the tables, Jesus is back in the temple teaching. The leaders ask, in effect: who ordained You?
The video explains semikhah, the laying on of hands to recognize a teacher, and says two witnesses were needed: John at the Jordan, and the Father's voice from heaven (John 8:18).
The Talmud's rule is three: 'From where do we derive that the ordination of elders is performed by three judges?' (Talmud Sanhedrin 13b). It grounds ordination in Moses laying hands on Joshua.

src.text: The baptism of John was from what source, from heaven or from men?” And they began reasoning among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will say to us, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From men,’ we fear the crowd; for they all regard John as a prophet.”

lines.text: Jesus' question is not a dodge. If John's baptism was from heaven, then the one John baptized and pointed to has heaven's authority.
They answer 'We do not know.' Leaders who should be guides are blind: 'they are blind guides of the blind' (15:14).

left.text: And he answered and said, ‘I will not’; but afterward he regretted it and went.

right.text: And the man came to the second and said the same thing; and he answered and said, ‘I will, sir’; but he did not go.

lines.text: 'A man had two sons' was a familiar way to open a story, as in Luke 15:11. The question: which one did the will of his father?
The message is doing the will of God (21:31). Compare 7:21: not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter.
The tax collectors and prostitutes believed John and repented. The leaders saw it and still did not regret afterward (21:32).

left.text: He dug it all around, removed its stones, / And planted it with the choicest vine. / And He built a tower in the middle of it / And also hewed out a wine vat in it; / Then He hoped for it to produce good grapes, / But it produced only worthless ones.

right.text: “Listen to another parable. There was a landowner who planted a vineyard and put a wall around it and dug a wine press in it, and built a tower, and rented it out to vine-growers and went on a journey.

lines.text: The wall, the wine press, the tower: Jesus is retelling Isaiah 5. Everyone listening would know the vineyard is Israel.
Psalm 80:8 uses the same picture: 'You removed a vine from Egypt; / You drove out the nations and then You planted it.'

src.text: For the vineyard of Yahweh of hosts is the house of Israel / And the men of Judah His delightful plant. / Thus He hoped for justice, but behold, bloodshed; / For righteousness, but behold, a cry of distress.

lines.text: In Hebrew the words sound alike: mishpat (justice) and mispach (bloodshed), tsedaqah (righteousness) and tse'aqah (a cry of distress). God looked for one and heard the other.
In Isaiah the vineyard itself is bad. In Jesus' parable the trouble is the vine-growers: the leaders put in charge of the vineyard.

src.text: But afterward he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But when the vine-growers saw the son, they said among themselves, ‘This is the heir; come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance.’ And they took him, and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

lines.text: The slaves are the prophets; the son is Jesus. Jesus is not indicting the people of Israel but the leaders who were supposed to care for the vineyard.
The video also suggests the tenants picture occupiers, as Rome and its appointed leaders held the land.
The leaders pronounce their own sentence: 'He will bring those wretches to a wretched end' (21:41).

left.text: The stone which the builders rejected / Has become the chief corner stone.

right.text: Jesus *said to them, “Did you never read in the Scriptures, / ‘The stone which the builders rejected, / This has become the chief corner stone; / This came about from the Lord, / And it is marvelous in our eyes’?

lines.text: The rejected son becomes the stone that holds the building together. The video pictures it as a capstone or cornerstone of protection.
This is the same psalm the crowds sang at the entry (118:26). The builders rejected what the people welcomed.

src.text: Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation, producing the fruit of it. And he who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; but on whomever it falls, it will scatter him like dust.”

lines.text: The same stone protects those who build on it and crushes those who oppose it.
'Producing the fruit of it' ties back to John's call to 'bear fruit in keeping with repentance' (3:8) and to the fig tree with leaves only (21:19).

src.text: And when the chief priests and the Pharisees heard His parables, they understood that He *was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to seize Him, they feared the crowds, because they were regarding Him to be a prophet.

lines.text: They understood the parable perfectly, and it made them want Him dead. This may be the parable that got Jesus killed.
Obedience and mercy are two sides of the same coin: 'If you had known what this means, “I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice”' (12:7).
So walk in Him: 'as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him' (Colossians 2:6). Faith without works is dead (James 2:26).

TERMS.def: The laying on of hands to ordain a teacher; the Talmud requires three (Sanhedrin 13b).
Lay leaders of the people, part of the Sanhedrin with the chief priests and scribes.
Tenant farmers who rented a vineyard and owed the owner part of the crop.
LSB 'chief corner stone' (Psalm 118:22); literally head of the corner, the key stone of a building.
The son who inherits; killing him was meant to seize the inheritance.

WORDS.gloss: Head of the corner; LSB 'chief corner stone.'
To winnow, scatter like chaff. Look up: BDAG, λικμάω.
Outcry, cry of distress (a pun on tsedaqah).

BACKGROUND.p: Absentee landowners in first-century Judea and Galilee often rented land to tenants for a share of the crop. A new vineyard took several years to bear, and disputes over payment were common, which makes the parable's setting realistic.

The Talmud discusses ordination ('semikhah') by laying on of hands: 'From where do we derive that the ordination of elders is performed by three judges?' (Talmud Sanhedrin 13b). How formal ordination was in Jesus' day is debated; the sources are later.
The crowds sang Psalm 118:26 as He entered. Now Jesus quotes 118:22 against the leaders. The same psalm frames both the welcome and the rejection.

WITNESSES.text: Therefore He brought in both harlots and publicans, that they might provoke them to jealousy.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 67, on 21:31-32. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Many things does He intimate by this parable, God's providence, which had been exercised towards them from the first; their murderous disposition from the beginning
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 68, on 21:33-41. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: Most read the vine-growers as Jerusalem's leaders, as 21:45 says. The video adds the idea of occupiers tied to Rome; that is an extension, not the text's own identification.

DEBATES.h: To whom is the kingdom given?
DEBATES.p: 'A nation producing the fruit of it' (21:43) has been read as the church of Jews and Gentiles, as the faithful remnant, or as new leaders over Israel. Matthew does not name it.
The Hebrew 'head of the corner' can mean a foundation cornerstone or a top stone. Translations differ; the LSB has 'chief corner stone.'

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says 'chief priests and scribes' come to Him; the LSB of 21:23 has 'the chief priests and the elders of the people,' and 21:45 has 'the chief priests and the Pharisees.'
The question about John's baptism is 21:25; the video says 21:2.
In 21:46 they were 'seeking to seize Him,' not just to find fault.
The video says ordination needed two rabbis. The Talmud's rule is three judges (Sanhedrin 13b), and how formal ordination was in Jesus' time is debated.
The idea that the chief stone was a capstone placed on parapets is offered without a source; the LSB reads 'chief corner stone.'
Psalm 118 has no title naming its author, so calling it a psalm of David is a tradition, not the text.

QUESTIONS: Why did Jesus answer the leaders with a question about John?
Which son are you more like, and where?
What would the first listeners hear when Jesus began to describe a wall, a wine press and a tower?
Why does the parable put the blame on the vine-growers rather than the vineyard?
How can the same stone be protection for some and destruction for others?
What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and knowing Him?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: to the one who knows God and obeys Him, Jesus Christ is the capstone or the cornerstone of protection. To the one who refuses to know God and disobeys His will, Jesus Christ will be the source of punishment and destruction. The dividing line runs between those who truly know God and those who only know religion. Obeying God is not a legalistic prerequisite for the kingdom; as James 2 says, good deeds are the evidence of faith. As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him (Colossians 2:6).

# Matthew 21:23-46 Study Notes: Is This the Parable That Got Jesus Killed?
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wZcIqDP6KEY
Channel: Every Word | Length: 28:00 | Series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)
Series hub: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/
Study page: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/matthew-42/
PDF for Goodnotes: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/assets/Matthew-Ep42-The-Stone-the-Builders-Rejected.pdf
Translation: Legacy Standard Bible (LSB). The video reads from another English translation; quotations here are LSB. Notes marked [Background] are added study helps, not from the video.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 21:23-46. In the temple the chief priests and elders demand to know by what authority Jesus acts. He answers with a question about John's baptism, and when they refuse to answer, so does He. Then He tells two parables. In the first, a man's two sons are told to work in the vineyard: one says no but goes, the other says yes but does not. In the second, a landowner plants a vineyard, rents it to vine-growers, and sends slaves and finally his son, whom they kill. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, 'The stone which the builders rejected,' and says the kingdom of God will be taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruit. The leaders realize He is speaking about them.
- The question about authority asks who gave Jesus the right to teach, the formal recognition of a rabbi. The crowds already saw that He taught as one having authority (7:28-29). Jesus points them to John, the prophet who baptized Him, and to the Father's voice from heaven.
- 'A man had two sons' was a known way to begin a story (Luke 15:11). The point: obedience, not words, is doing the will of the Father. Tax collectors and prostitutes, who said no and then repented, are entering the kingdom before the leaders.
- The vineyard parable is built on Isaiah 5, where Israel is God's vineyard and God looks for justice and finds bloodshed. Here the problem is the vine-growers, the leaders. Psalm 118:22 turns the rejected son into the chief corner stone.
- The lesson: to the one who knows God and obeys Him, Jesus Christ is the cornerstone of protection. To the one who refuses to know God and disobeys His will, Jesus Christ will be the source of punishment and destruction.

## Key quotes from the video (auto-captions, lightly cleaned)
> "To the one who knows God and obeys him, Jesus Christ is the capstone or the cornerstone of protection."
> "Putting both parables together, the message becomes clear. It's doing the will of God."
> "Jesus indicts the ones who were supposed to care for this vineyard."
> "It reveals the dividing line between those who truly know God and those who only know religion."

### Find the Old Testament story under the parable
Jesus' vineyard parable retells Isaiah 5:1-7 and ends with Psalm 118:22. Reading those first shows who the vineyard, the owner, the tenants and the son are.

   (video) So walk in Him: 'as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him' (Colossians 2:6). Faith without works is dead (James 2:26). (James 2:26)

## Key people
- The chief priests and elders: Challenge His authority; represented by the vine-growers. [Background] In 21:45 Matthew names the chief priests and Pharisees as the listeners who understood.
- John the Baptist: The prophet whose baptism was from heaven, a witness to Jesus. [Background] The crowds all regarded him as a prophet (21:26).
- The two sons: One says no and goes; one says yes and does not. [Background] Only Matthew has this parable.
- Tax collectors and prostitutes: Said no to God, then repented at John's preaching. [Background] Compare Luke 3:12; 7:29-30.
- The landowner, slaves and son: God, the prophets, and Jesus. [Background] Mark 12:1-12 and Luke 20:9-19 tell the same parable.
- The vine-growers: The leaders who should have tended God's vineyard. [Background] They reason, 'This is the heir' (21:38).

## Places [Background]
- Jerusalem (named in the video): The temple, where He is asked 'By what authority?' (21:23).
- Bethany beyond the Jordan: Where John was baptizing (John 1:28); site traditional.

## Key terms
- Semikhah: The laying on of hands to ordain a teacher; the Talmud requires three (Sanhedrin 13b).
- Elders: Lay leaders of the people, part of the Sanhedrin with the chief priests and scribes. [Background]
- Vine-growers: Tenant farmers who rented a vineyard and owed the owner part of the crop.
- Chief corner stone: LSB 'chief corner stone' (Psalm 118:22); literally head of the corner, the key stone of a building.
- Heir: The son who inherits; killing him was meant to seize the inheritance. [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Tenant vineyards: Absentee landowners in first-century Judea and Galilee often rented land to tenants for a share of the crop. A new vineyard took several years to bear, and disputes over payment were common, which makes the parable's setting realistic.
- Ordination in the sources: The Talmud discusses ordination ('semikhah') by laying on of hands: 'From where do we derive that the ordination of elders is performed by three judges?' (Talmud Sanhedrin 13b). How formal ordination was in Jesus' day is debated; the sources are later.
- Psalm 118 in the week: The crowds sang Psalm 118:26 as He entered. Now Jesus quotes 118:22 against the leaders. The same psalm frames both the welcome and the rejection.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Therefore He brought in both harlots and publicans, that they might provoke them to jealousy." Homilies on Matthew 67, on 21:31-32. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Many things does He intimate by this parable, God's providence, which had been exercised towards them from the first; their murderous disposition from the beginning" Homilies on Matthew 68, on 21:33-41. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who are the tenants? Most read the vine-growers as Jerusalem's leaders, as 21:45 says. The video adds the idea of occupiers tied to Rome; that is an extension, not the text's own identification.
- To whom is the kingdom given? 'A nation producing the fruit of it' (21:43) has been read as the church of Jews and Gentiles, as the faithful remnant, or as new leaders over Israel. Matthew does not name it.
- Cornerstone or capstone? The Hebrew 'head of the corner' can mean a foundation cornerstone or a top stone. Translations differ; the LSB has 'chief corner stone.'

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says 'chief priests and scribes' come to Him; the LSB of 21:23 has 'the chief priests and the elders of the people,' and 21:45 has 'the chief priests and the Pharisees.'
- The question about John's baptism is 21:25; the video says 21:2.
- In 21:46 they were 'seeking to seize Him,' not just to find fault.
- The video says ordination needed two rabbis. The Talmud's rule is three judges (Sanhedrin 13b), and how formal ordination was in Jesus' time is debated.
- The idea that the chief stone was a capstone placed on parapets is offered without a source; the LSB reads 'chief corner stone.'
- Psalm 118 has no title naming its author, so calling it a psalm of David is a tradition, not the text.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why did Jesus answer the leaders with a question about John?
2. Which son are you more like, and where?
3. What would the first listeners hear when Jesus began to describe a wall, a wine press and a tower?
4. Why does the parable put the blame on the vine-growers rather than the vineyard?
5. How can the same stone be protection for some and destruction for others?
6. What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and knowing Him?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: to the one who knows God and obeys Him, Jesus Christ is the capstone or the cornerstone of protection. To the one who refuses to know God and disobeys His will, Jesus Christ will be the source of punishment and destruction. The dividing line runs between those who truly know God and those who only know religion. Obeying God is not a legalistic prerequisite for the kingdom; as James 2 says, good deeds are the evidence of faith. As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him (Colossians 2:6).
- Study note (added): name one thing you have told God 'I will, sir' about and not done. Take the first step on it this week, and tell one person so they can ask you about it.
